newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks reform of Western resource subsidies.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks reform of Western resource subsidies.

text.p: The White House signalled Monday that it would try again to reform subsidies for exploiting resources from federal lands, an issue on which it was bruised in President Bill Clinton's first term.

In the annual "Economic Report of the President," the administration said policies for activities such as grazing, logging, mining and water projects must be changed to reflect the West's changing economy and to accommodate competing interests in the increasingly diverse region.

"The Administration is committed to ensuring that natural resource policies reflect today's realities and balance the diverse and sometimes competing objectives of all who derive benefits from the natural environment," the report, prepared by Clinton's Council of Economic Advisers, said.

In Clinton's first term, Western lawmakers in Congress shot down the administration's attempts to hike grazing and mining fees and succeeded in making the administration reopen logging in some sensitive areas.
In the new report, the administration criticised current subsidies as being environmentally destructive and rooted in old policies to encourage settlement of the West.
It said policies should be changed to reflect market values and give conservationists and other interests a chance to bid on resources.
Rights for mining, grazing and other activities should be more transferable and "more exposed to market signals," the report said.

"By encouraging overinvestment and overproduction in the livestock, mining and timber industries, subsidies attract resources away from other, more productive sectors of the economy and reduce overall economic well-being," it said.
"Reducing subsidies can improve economic performance by giving producers better information about the true cost of using public land," it added.

While some communities oppose letting conservation interests get extraction rights because that would threaten local companies and development, the report said those businesses would fade anyway as the economy diversifies and shifts from activities such as mining and logging.

Reducing subsidies and relying more on market mechanisms also would help lower the deficit, the report said. For example, it said, the Interior Department calculated that an 8 percent net income royalty on hardrock minerals from federal lands would generate at least $275 million over five years.
If grazing permits were auctioned competitively, the report said, more money likely would be generated than would be generated through the grazing fee increases the administration proposed in 1994.
The current patenting process for mining could be replaced with a system of royalties and competitive bidding on bonus payments to the government to generate more revenue, it said.
While timber contracts are awarded on a competitive basis, the report said contracts should be revised to reduce federal losses on road-building and other expenses in national forests.
